retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract shift/rotate-then-compare; no task-specific parameters.

retrieved_cards.title: Compared against a one-way digest: do NOT try to invert it
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: The input is compared against a fixed-length, high-entropy constant produced by a one-way function (hash/checksum); the transform is not reversible.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: Unlike invertible encodings, a digest cannot be reversed to the input; the visible digest is the comparison target, submitting it raw fails, and inverting it is also futile.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Identify the function as one-way; redirect effort to finding or constraining the pre-image rather than inverting; confirm a candidate by computing the digest of the candidate yourself and checking it equals the compared constant.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Submit the digest, or attempt to 'decrypt'/invert the hash to recover the input.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Recognize a one-way function: the accepted input must be found another way (located in the binary/inputs, or recovered by a constrained search), not by inverting the digest.
not_applicable_when: the transform is actually reversible (XOR/shift/encoding -- use the matching card and invert)
the constant is not a digest of the input
misfire_risks: mislabeling a reversible transform as one-way stops a valid inversion; distinguish a true digest (fixed length, avalanche) from an invertible encoding before abandoning inversion
minimum_evidence_before_use: the comparison target is a fixed-length high-entropy constant
the producing function matches a known one-way construction

retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract shift/rotate-then-compare; no task-specific parameters.

retrieved_cards.title: Compared against a one-way digest: do NOT try to invert it
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: The input is compared against a fixed-length, high-entropy constant produced by a one-way function (hash/checksum); the transform is not reversible.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: Unlike invertible encodings, a digest cannot be reversed to the input; the visible digest is the comparison target, submitting it raw fails, and inverting it is also futile.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Identify the function as one-way; redirect effort to finding or constraining the pre-image rather than inverting; confirm a candidate by computing the digest of the candidate yourself and checking it equals the compared constant.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: Submit the digest, or attempt to 'decrypt'/invert the hash to recover the input.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Recognize a one-way function: the accepted input must be found another way (located in the binary/inputs, or recovered by a constrained search), not by inverting the digest.
not_applicable_when: the transform is actually reversible (XOR/shift/encoding -- use the matching card and invert)
the constant is not a digest of the input
misfire_risks: mislabeling a reversible transform as one-way stops a valid inversion; distinguish a true digest (fixed length, avalanche) from an invertible encoding before abandoning inversion
minimum_evidence_before_use: the comparison target is a fixed-length high-entropy constant
the producing function matches a known one-way construction

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract one-way-digest counter-case; no task-specific hashes or constants.

retrieved_cards.title: XOR-then-compare: recover the input by XORing the target back
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A byte-wise XOR with a constant (single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent key) is applied to the input before it is compared against a constant byte sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: XOR is its own inverse; the compared bytes are input XOR key, so the visible target is the encoded form, not the input.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Read the key and whether it is single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent; XOR the target back; then XOR the recovered input forward again and check it reproduces the compared bytes exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The XORed/compared bytes are the flag, or the check is 'encrypted' and not worth pursuing.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: XOR the comparison target back with the same key to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no XOR appears on the comparison path
the XOR is applied to an unrelated buffer, not the input being checked
misfire_risks: the key may be position-dependent / rolling rather than a single constant byte; assuming a single-byte key yields a wrong pre-image -- verify the key schedule before inverting
minimum_evidence_before_use: an XOR operation is observed between the input and the comparison
the XOR operand (key) is identifiable or recoverable

Each iteration, it reads a 64-bit value from that table, divides by 19 to get the opcode index, and calls the corresponding function. Looking at the functions: op0 does a complex operation, op1 throws, op2 adds, op3 subtracts, op4 multiplies... The VM manipulates the input stored at 0x63bb20 and compares with target at 0x4040a0. args.code:
# Let's understand the VM better by parsing the bytecode/program
# and simulating it to understand the transformation

import struct

# Read the binary
with open("{TARGET}", "rb") as f:
    data = f.read()

# Extract the program at 0x404180 (virtual address, need to find file offset)
# From objdump/readelf: .data section starts at 0x404080
# Let's find the offset

# For stripped binary, let's find the data directly
# The target comparison data is at 0x4040a0 (64 bytes)
# The function table is at 0x4040e0 (19 pointers)
# The program is at 0x404180

# Find by looking at the section headers
# Assuming PIE is not used (it's an executable), file offset = virtual - base
# Typical base for .data is near 0x404000, let's compute offset

# From the binary, let's extract using patterns we know
# The function pointers start with 0x4011d6 which is 0xd6 0x11 0x40 0x00 ...

# Search for the function pointer table
pattern = b'\xd6\x11\x40\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00'
idx = data.find(pattern)
print(f"Found function table at file offset: {hex(idx)}")

# The virtual address is 0x4040e0, so base offset is idx - 0x4040e0 + virtual_base
# But simpler: idx corresponds to 0x4040e0
# So 0x4040a0 is at idx - (0x4040e0 - 0x4040a0) = idx - 0x40

target_offset = idx - 0x40
print(f"Target data at file offset: {hex(target_offset)}")
target_data = data[target_offset:target_offset+64]
print(f"Target (comparison) data:")
print(target_data.hex())

# The program is at 0x404180, which is idx + (0x404180 - 0x4040e0) = idx + 0xa0
program_offset = idx + 0xa0
print(f"\nProgram at file offset: {hex(program_offset)}")

# Let's read the program - it's a series of 64-bit values
# Each value when divided by 19 gives opcode, and has an operand
program = []
for i in range(256):  # Read 256 instructions
    off = program_offset + i * 8
    if off + 8 > len(data):
        break
    val = struct.unpack('<Q', data[off:off+8])[0]
    program.append(val)
    if val % 19 == 18:  # Halt opcode
        print(f"Halt found at instruction {i}")
        break

print(f"\nProgram has {len(program)} instructions")

# Now let's decode the instructions
print("\nDecoded program (first 50 instructions):")
opcodes = {
    0: "LOAD_IMM",   # loads next instruction's operand
    1: "THROW",      # throws exception 
    2: "ADD",        # acc0 += acc1
    3: "SUB",        # acc0 -= acc1
    4: "MUL",        # acc0 *= acc1
    5: "AND",        # acc0 &= acc1
    6: "XOR",        # acc0 ^= acc1
    7: "OR",         # acc0 |= acc1
    8: "SHL",        # acc0 <<= (acc1 & 0x3f)
    9: "SHR",        # acc0 >>= (acc1 & 0x3f)
    10: "COPY",      # acc1 = acc0 (store to reg)
    11: "SWAP",      # swap acc0, acc1
    12: "LOAD_PROG", # loads from program using next instr
    13: "LOAD_INP",  # acc0 = input[acc0]
    14: "STORE_INP", # input[acc0] = acc1
    15: "CMP_EQ",    # acc1 = (acc0 == acc1) ? 1 : 0
    16: "NOP1",
    17: "NOP2",
    18: "HALT",
}

for i, val in enumerate(program[:50]):
    opcode = val % 19
    operand = val // 19
    print(f"{i:3}: {opcodes.get(opcode, '?'):12} (raw={val:#018x}, op={opcode}, operand={operand:#x})")

retrieved_cards.title: XOR-then-compare: recover the input by XORing the target back
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A byte-wise XOR with a constant (single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent key) is applied to the input before it is compared against a constant byte sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: XOR is its own inverse; the compared bytes are input XOR key, so the visible target is the encoded form, not the input.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Read the key and whether it is single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent; XOR the target back; then XOR the recovered input forward again and check it reproduces the compared bytes exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The XORed/compared bytes are the flag, or the check is 'encrypted' and not worth pursuing.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: XOR the comparison target back with the same key to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no XOR appears on the comparison path
the XOR is applied to an unrelated buffer, not the input being checked
misfire_risks: the key may be position-dependent / rolling rather than a single constant byte; assuming a single-byte key yields a wrong pre-image -- verify the key schedule before inverting
minimum_evidence_before_use: an XOR operation is observed between the input and the comparison
the XOR operand (key) is identifiable or recoverable

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract XOR-then-compare; no task-specific keys, constants, or symbols.

retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

retrieved_cards.title: XOR-then-compare: recover the input by XORing the target back
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A byte-wise XOR with a constant (single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent key) is applied to the input before it is compared against a constant byte sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: XOR is its own inverse; the compared bytes are input XOR key, so the visible target is the encoded form, not the input.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Read the key and whether it is single-byte, repeating, or position-dependent; XOR the target back; then XOR the recovered input forward again and check it reproduces the compared bytes exactly.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The XORed/compared bytes are the flag, or the check is 'encrypted' and not worth pursuing.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: XOR the comparison target back with the same key to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no XOR appears on the comparison path
the XOR is applied to an unrelated buffer, not the input being checked
misfire_risks: the key may be position-dependent / rolling rather than a single constant byte; assuming a single-byte key yields a wrong pre-image -- verify the key schedule before inverting
minimum_evidence_before_use: an XOR operation is observed between the input and the comparison
the XOR operand (key) is identifiable or recoverable

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract XOR-then-compare; no task-specific keys, constants, or symbols.

retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.

retrieved_cards.title: A success branch under a constant/macro guard is dead
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A branch that prints success or the flag is guarded by a condition that is constant at runtime via a literal or build macro (e.g. if(0), #ifdef DEBUG with DEBUG unset, a global never set true) -- readable as constant by inspection.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A statically-constant guard is overlooked, so a never-taken success branch is read as a live path to the flag.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the guard's value from the code (constant literal, build macro, or a global with no writer anywhere in the binary); a branch under a constant-false guard is dead and its contents are not evidence.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: This branch prints the flag / 'correct', so reaching it (or reading its contents) yields the answer.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the guard: if it is constant-false via a literal or macro, the branch is dead and its contents do not gate acceptance.
not_applicable_when: the guard is a computed expression that only looks constant (that is decompiler_artifact / opaque-predicate, not this card)
the guard depends on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a guard that appears constant in one build may be configurable; confirm it in the disassembly, and check for writers to the global, rather than assuming from a source-like reconstruction
minimum_evidence_before_use: a success/flag branch is gated by a literal- or macro-constant condition

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract constant-guard dead-branch pattern; no task specifics. Distinct from opaque-predicate (computed) which is decompiler_artifact.

retrieved_cards.title: A variable/field name asserts contents it may not hold
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A data symbol whose name asserts its contents -- a validity result, a key, a credential, the answer -- is being trusted to hold what the name implies, without confirming what is actually stored or how it is used.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A data symbol's name is conflated with the value it actually holds; a symbol named for the answer may hold a decoy, a transformed value, or be unrelated to acceptance.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Enumerate the writers of the symbol and the values they can store; confirm the accepting branch reads it before trusting its name.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The symbol named for the key or the answer holds it, so read or submit its value.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Find every writer of the variable and what it can hold at the point of use, and whether the accepting branch depends on it; the name is not a guarantee.
not_applicable_when: the variable's contents and role have been confirmed
symbols are stripped
misfire_risks: over-doubt can waste effort on obviously-named locals; reserve for cases where the variable drives or appears to drive acceptance
minimum_evidence_before_use: a semantically-named data symbol is present
its contents/role are unconfirmed

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract data-symbol-name over-trust; no task specifics. W10b: literal example identifiers replaced with the semantic category they stood for; the names happened to coincide with identifiers present in the eval ground truth / archetype source.

retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract shift/rotate-then-compare; no task-specific parameters.

1. __cxa_begin_catch is called
2. RBX is added to PC at [0x63bb08]

4. Jump back to loop

So after each opcode, PC is incremented by the value in RBX. But where is RBX set?
Looking at the opcode functions, RBX is used to hold the exception object.
Wait, RBX might come from the exception itself or be set before the call.

Actually, in the main loop:
- RBP holds the function table pointer (0x4040e0)
- RBX might hold the PC increment value

Let me check: RBX is pushed at the start (0x401862). It might be set somewhere before the loop starts. The loop iterates but RBX might be a constant like 1 or 2 depending on opcode.

retrieved_cards.title: A success branch under a constant/macro guard is dead
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A branch that prints success or the flag is guarded by a condition that is constant at runtime via a literal or build macro (e.g. if(0), #ifdef DEBUG with DEBUG unset, a global never set true) -- readable as constant by inspection.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A statically-constant guard is overlooked, so a never-taken success branch is read as a live path to the flag.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the guard's value from the code (constant literal, build macro, or a global with no writer anywhere in the binary); a branch under a constant-false guard is dead and its contents are not evidence.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: This branch prints the flag / 'correct', so reaching it (or reading its contents) yields the answer.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the guard: if it is constant-false via a literal or macro, the branch is dead and its contents do not gate acceptance.
not_applicable_when: the guard is a computed expression that only looks constant (that is decompiler_artifact / opaque-predicate, not this card)
the guard depends on input and the branch is genuinely reachable
misfire_risks: a guard that appears constant in one build may be configurable; confirm it in the disassembly, and check for writers to the global, rather than assuming from a source-like reconstruction
minimum_evidence_before_use: a success/flag branch is gated by a literal- or macro-constant condition

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract constant-guard dead-branch pattern; no task specifics. Distinct from opaque-predicate (computed) which is decompiler_artifact.

retrieved_cards.title: A variable/field name asserts contents it may not hold
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: A data symbol whose name asserts its contents -- a validity result, a key, a credential, the answer -- is being trusted to hold what the name implies, without confirming what is actually stored or how it is used.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: A data symbol's name is conflated with the value it actually holds; a symbol named for the answer may hold a decoy, a transformed value, or be unrelated to acceptance.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Enumerate the writers of the symbol and the values they can store; confirm the accepting branch reads it before trusting its name.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The symbol named for the key or the answer holds it, so read or submit its value.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Find every writer of the variable and what it can hold at the point of use, and whether the accepting branch depends on it; the name is not a guarantee.
not_applicable_when: the variable's contents and role have been confirmed
symbols are stripped
misfire_risks: over-doubt can waste effort on obviously-named locals; reserve for cases where the variable drives or appears to drive acceptance
minimum_evidence_before_use: a semantically-named data symbol is present
its contents/role are unconfirmed

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract data-symbol-name over-trust; no task specifics. W10b: literal example identifiers replaced with the semantic category they stood for; the names happened to coincide with identifiers present in the eval ground truth / archetype source.

retrieved_cards.title: Shift/rotate-then-compare: apply the inverse shift to recover the input
retrieved_cards.applicability_signal: Each input byte is shifted, added/subtracted, or bit-rotated by a constant (Caesar/ROT/byte-rotate) before comparison against a constant sequence.
retrieved_cards.mechanism: An additive or rotational transform maps the input to the compared form; the visible target is the shifted input, recoverable by the inverse operation.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the shift amount and the domain (full byte mod 256 vs a restricted alphabet), apply the inverse, then re-apply the forward shift to the result and check it reproduces the compared sequence byte for byte.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: The shifted/compared sequence is the flag.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Apply the inverse shift/rotation (matching the modulus and alphabet used) to the target to recover the accepted input.
not_applicable_when: no constant per-byte shift/rotate is present on the path
the operation is data-dependent rather than a constant shift (treat as a general transform / solve instead)
misfire_risks: the modulus and alphabet matter: assuming full-byte mod 256 when the code wraps within a restricted alphabet (or vice-versa) yields a wrong pre-image
minimum_evidence_before_use: a constant per-byte shift or rotation is observed on the comparison path

provenance.authoring_note: Abstract shift/rotate-then-compare; no task-specific parameters.

retrieval_event.query:
Found the exception handler! At 0x4018d7-0x4018eb:
1. __cxa_begin_catch is called
2. RBX is added to PC at [0x63bb08]
3. __cxa_end_catch is called
4. Jump back to loop

So after each opcode, PC is incremented by the value in RBX. But where is RBX set?
Looking at the opcode functions, RBX is used to hold the exception object.
Wait, RBX might come from the exception itself or be set before the call.

Actually, in the main loop:
- RBP holds the function table pointer (0x4040e0)
- RBX might hold the PC increment value

Let me check: RBX is pushed at the start (0x401862). It might be set somewhere before the loop starts. The loop iterates but RBX might be a constant like 1 or 2 depending on opcode.

retrieved_cards.mechanism: A statically-constant guard is overlooked, so a never-taken success branch is read as a live path to the flag.
retrieved_cards.validation_note: Determine the guard's value from the code (constant literal, build macro, or a global with no writer anywhere in the binary); a branch under a constant-false guard is dead and its contents are not evidence.
retrieved_cards.misleading_interpretation: This branch prints the flag / 'correct', so reaching it (or reading its contents) yields the answer.
retrieved_cards.better_interpretation: Evaluate the guard: if it is constant-false via a literal or macro, the branch is dead and its contents do not gate acceptance.

idx = data.find(pattern)

target = struct.unpack('<8Q', data[target_offset:target_offset+64])

for i, v in enumerate(target):

# Key observation: the VM has an exception-based flow where:
# 1. Each opcode does some work on stack slots
# 2. Throws an exception
# 3. Exception handler increments PC and loops

# RBX must hold 1 for most opcodes, 2 for LOAD_IMM

# __cxa_allocate_exception -> mov rbx, rax

# Or maybe the mechanism is different.

# The LSDA (Language-Specific Data Area) mentioned in the FDE entries
# determines HOW exceptions are handled.

# Looking at op0 (0x4011d6-0x40123a):

#   ...
#   mov rbx, rax     ; rbx = exception ptr
#   ...
#   call __cxa_throw ; throws, rbx is still exception ptr
#   (landing pad)
#   mov rbx, rdi     ; actually no, looking at 0x401227: mov rbp, rax
#   call __cxa_free_exception
#   call _Unwind_Resume

# After unwinding past the opcode function, caller's RBX is restored.

# 0x401861: push rbp
# 0x401862: push rbx
# 0x401863: sub rsp, 8
# 0x401867: lea rbp, [0x4040e0]   ; rbp = function table
# 0x40186e: (loop starts)

# 0x4019fb: call fcn.00401861
#
# RBX is pushed at 0x40196a but also not initialized!
# It's whatever __libc_start_main set.

# anything specific before calling main.

# BUT WAIT! I just noticed something crucial.
# Each opcode function starts with:
#   push r12
#   push rbp
#   push rbx
#
# So after these 3 pushes, RSP is reduced by 24 bytes.
# Inside the opcode, [rsp - 0x1000] refers to a location that is
# DIFFERENT from what it would be in the caller!

# The opcodes use [rsp - 0x1000], [rsp - 0xff0], [rsp - 0xfe0] as slots.
# These are 16 bytes apart (0x10).

# After the call from main loop to opcode:
# - Main loop's RSP is at some address X
# - After call (push return addr): RSP = X - 8
# - After push r12, push rbp, push rbx: RSP = X - 8 - 24 = X - 32

# [rsp - 0x1000] = [X - 32 - 0x1000] = [X - 0x1020]
# [rsp - 0xff0]  = [X - 32 - 0xff0]  = [X - 0x1010]
# [rsp - 0xfe0]  = [X - 32 - 0xfe0]  = [X - 0x1000]

# Inside main loop (before call):
# [rsp - 0x1020] would be... well, main loop RSP is different from main's RSP.

# Let me think about stack layout:
# main() at 0x40196a:
#   push rbx        ; RSP -= 8
#   sub rsp, 0x20   ; RSP -= 32
#   ; RSP is now main_entry - 40 = main_rsp
#
# fcn.00401861() at 0x401861:
#   ; called from main, return addr pushed, RSP = main_rsp - 8
#   push rbp        ; RSP -= 8
#   push rbx        ; RSP -= 8
#   sub rsp, 8      ; RSP -= 8
#   ; RSP is now main_rsp - 32 = vm_rsp
#
# opcode function:
#   ; called from VM loop, return addr pushed, RSP = vm_rsp - 8
#   push r12        ; RSP -= 8
#   push rbp        ; RSP -= 8
#   push rbx        ; RSP -= 8
#   ; RSP is now vm_rsp - 32 = op_rsp
#
# Inside opcode:

# [op_rsp - 0xff0]  = [vm_rsp - 0x1010]
# [op_rsp - 0xfe0]  = [vm_rsp - 0x1000]

# slot2 = [vm_rsp - 0x1000]

# Looking at op12 (LOAD_PROG at 0x40162b):
# 1. rsi = [0x404170] = 0x404180 (program base)
# 2. rdi = [0x63bb08] = PC
# 3. rcx = [rsi + rdi*8 + 8] = program[PC+1]
# 4. rcx = rcx + rcx = 2 * program[PC+1]
# 5. rax = [rsp - 0xff0] (address of the stack slot area)
# 6. rdx = [rax + rcx*8] = value from stack slot indexed by 2*program[PC+1]
# 7. [rsp - 0x1000] = rdx (store to slot0)

# So op12 loads from a COMPUTED slot position based on program[PC+1].
# The index is 2 * program[PC+1], then multiplied by 8 for qword access.

# This suggests there's an ARRAY of slots, not just 3!
# The base is [rsp - 0xff0], and index can vary.

# Now looking at op13 (LOAD_INP at 0x40169f):
# 1. rax = [rsp - 0xff0] (slot1)
# 2. rdx = [rax*8 + 0x63bb20] = input[slot1]
# 3. [rsp - 0xff0] = rdx (slot1 = input[slot1])

# So op13 uses slot1 as an index into the input array, then stores back to slot1.

# And op14 (STORE_INP at 0x401700):
# 1. rax = [rsp - 0xff0] (slot1)
# 2. rdx = [rsp - 0xfe0] (slot2)
# 3. [rax*8 + 0x63bb20] = rdx (input[slot1] = slot2)

# So op14 stores slot2 into input[slot1].

# Now I understand better! The VM uses:
# - slot1 ([rsp - 0xff0]) and slot2 ([rsp - 0xfe0]) for most operations
# - slot0 ([rsp - 0x1000]) for loading immediates and intermediate results
# - Input array at 0x63bb20 (8 quadwords)

# The question remains: how does a value move from slot0 to slot1/slot2?
# 
# Wait, I just realized: the slots are at fixed OFFSETS from RSP.
# Inside each opcode, RSP is the same (after pushes).
# So:
# [rsp - 0x1000] = a fixed address for ALL opcodes (the same location!)
# [rsp - 0xff0] = another fixed address 
# [rsp - 0xfe0] = another fixed address

# They're NOT different locations for different opcodes - they're THE SAME!

# So:
# vm_rsp = RSP in main VM loop
# After call and 3 pushes: op_rsp = vm_rsp - 8 - 24 = vm_rsp - 32

# For ALL opcodes:
# slot0 = [op_rsp - 0x1000] = [vm_rsp - 0x1020]
# slot1 = [op_rsp - 0xff0]  = [vm_rsp - 0x1010]
# slot2 = [op_rsp - 0xfe0]  = [vm_rsp - 0x1000]

# These are just 3 fixed memory locations! They persist across opcode calls.
# Values stay in the slots until overwritten.

# Now re-tracing the VM with correct slot semantics:
# PC=0: LOAD_IMM -> slot0 = program[1] = 0
# PC=2: LOAD_IMM -> slot0 = program[3] = 0x874b1456b185272f
# PC=4: LOAD_IMM -> slot0 = program[5] = 0xa75d27d98fba6cc2 (wait, this is instruction 5, not immediate!)

# Hmm, the immediate for LOAD_IMM at PC=4 is program[5].
# But instruction at index 5 is: 0xa75d27d98fba6cc2, opcode=7 (OR).

# Wait, I think the instruction stream is interleaved with immediates!
# Let me re-decode:

import struct

with open("{TARGET}", "rb") as f:
    data = f.read()

pattern = b'\xd6\x11\x40\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00'
idx = data.find(pattern)
program_offset = idx + 0xa0

program = []
for i in range(50):
    off = program_offset + i * 8
    val = struct.unpack('<Q', data[off:off+8])[0]
    program.append(val)

# Trace with proper immediate handling
slot0 = 0
slot1 = 0
slot2 = 0
input_arr = [f'inp{i}' for i in range(8)]
pc = 0

op_names = {
    0: "LOAD_IMM",
    1: "NOP1",
    2: "ADD",
    3: "SUB", 
    4: "MUL",
    5: "AND",
    6: "XOR",
    7: "OR",
    8: "SHL",
    9: "SHR",
    10: "COPY",
    11: "SWAP",
    12: "LOAD_PROG",
    13: "LOAD_INP",
    14: "STORE_INP",
    15: "CMP_EQ",
    16: "NOP2",
    17: "NOP3",
    18: "HALT",
}

print("VM Trace (correct model):")
while pc < len(program):
    instr = program[pc]
    opcode = instr % 19
    
    if opcode == 18:  # HALT
        print(f"PC={pc}: HALT")
        break
    
    if opcode == 0:  # LOAD_IMM
        imm = program[pc + 1] if pc + 1 < len(program) else 0
        slot0 = imm
        print(f"PC={pc}: LOAD_IMM slot0 = {imm:#018x}")
        pc += 2
    elif opcode in [1, 16, 17]:  # NOPs
        print(f"PC={pc}: NOP")
        pc += 1
    elif opcode == 2:  # ADD
        slot2 = (slot2 + slot1) & ((1<<64)-1) if isinstance(slot2, int) and isinstance(slot1, int) else f"({slot2})+({slot1})"
        print(f"PC={pc}: ADD slot2 = slot2 + slot1 -> {slot2 if isinstance(slot2, str) else hex(slot2)}")
        pc += 1
    elif opcode == 3:  # SUB
        slot2 = (slot2 - slot1) & ((1<<64)-1) if isinstance(slot2, int) and isinstance(slot1, int) else f"({slot2})-({slot1})"
        print(f"PC={pc}: SUB slot2 = slot2 - slot1 -> {slot2 if isinstance(slot2, str) else hex(slot2)}")
        pc += 1
    elif opcode == 7:  # OR
        slot2 = (slot2 | slot1) if isinstance(slot2, int) and isinstance(slot1, int) else f"({slot2})|({slot1})"
        print(f"PC={pc}: OR slot2 = slot2 | slot1 -> {slot2 if isinstance(slot2, str) else hex(slot2)}")
        pc += 1
    elif opcode == 9:  # SHR
        shift = (slot1 & 0x3f) if isinstance(slot1, int) else slot1
        slot2 = (slot2 >> shift) if isinstance(slot2, int) and isinstance(shift, int) else f"({slot2})>>{shift}"
        print(f"PC={pc}: SHR slot2 = slot2 >> (slot1 & 0x3f)")
        pc += 1
    elif opcode == 11:  # SWAP
        slot1, slot2 = slot2, slot1
        print(f"PC={pc}: SWAP slot1 <-> slot2")
        pc += 1
    elif opcode == 12:  # LOAD_PROG
        idx_val = program[pc + 1] if pc + 1 < len(program) else 0
        # Load from [base + 2*idx_val*8] where base is slot array
        # This is complex - let's skip for now
        print(f"PC={pc}: LOAD_PROG (complex) idx={idx_val}")
        pc += 2
    elif opcode == 13:  # LOAD_INP
        if isinstance(slot1, int):
            idx = slot1 & 7
            slot1 = input_arr[idx]
            print(f"PC={pc}: LOAD_INP slot1 = input[{idx}] = {slot1}")
        else:
            print(f"PC={pc}: LOAD_INP slot1 = input[{slot1}]")
        pc += 1
    elif opcode == 14:  # STORE_INP
        if isinstance(slot1, int):
            idx = slot1 & 7
            input_arr[idx] = slot2
            print(f"PC={pc}: STORE_INP input[{idx}] = slot2 = {slot2 if isinstance(slot2, str) else hex(slot2)}")
        else:
            print(f"PC={pc}: STORE_INP input[{slot1}] = slot2")
        pc += 1
    elif opcode == 15:  # CMP_EQ
        result = (1 if slot2 == slot1 else 0) if isinstance(slot2, int) and isinstance(slot1, int) else f"({slot2})==({slot1})"
        slot2 = result
        print(f"PC={pc}: CMP_EQ slot2 = (slot2 == slot1) -> {slot2}")
